ASSAYING SILVER IN SILVER AND 

SILVER ALLOYS — METHODS 

( Second Revision ) 



ICS 77.120.01, 39.060 



O BIS 2002 

BUREAU OF INDIAN STANDARDS 

MANAK BHAVAN, 9 BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR MARG 
NEW DELHI 110002 

December 2002 Price Clroup 4 



Precious Metals Sectional Committee, MTD 10 



FOREWORD 

This Indian Standard (Second Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized 
by the Precious Metals Sectional Committee, had been approved by the Metallurgical Engineering Division 
Council. 

The methods are intended to determine fineness of silver in silver and silver alloys as covered in IS 21 12 : 2002 
^Silver, jewellery/artifacts — Fineness and marking — Specification' except for fineness of 999.9. 

While revising this standard need was felt to align the test methods with prescribed International Standards. 
The additional Gravimetric Method II incorporated during this revision is based on ISO 11427 : 1993. This 
standard, therefore, has been aligned with the International Standards. 

The composition of the Committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 

In reporting the result of a test or analysis in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 'Rules for rounding off numerical 
values (revised)'.

18 2113:2002 



Indian Standard 

ASSAYING SILVER IN SILVER AND 
SILVER ALLOYS — METHODS 

( Second Revision ) 



I SCOPE 



1.1 This standard prescribes the methods for 
determination of silver in silver alloys as below: 

a) Gravimetric Method I (Bottle Assay) and 
Method II 

b) Volumetric ( Potentiometric) Method. 

The methods are suitable for determination of silver 
in the ranges as specified in IS 2 1 1 2 except for fineness 
999.9 for which the test method may be agreed to 
between the parties concerned since there associated 
impurities have to be determined. The silver alloys 
may contain Cu, Zn, Cd and Pd. These elements except 
palladium, which must be precipitated before titration, 
do not interfere with this method of determination of 
silver. 

The volumetric method can be used for silver of 
fineness 99.5 percent and below. These alloys may 
contain copper, zinc, cadmium and palladium. These 
elements, except palladium, which must be 
precipitated before titration, do not interfere with this 
method of determination of silver. 

2 REFERENCES 

The standards listed below contain provisions which 
through reference in this text, constitute provisions of 
this standard. At the time of publication, the editions 
indicated were valid. All standards are subject to 
revision and parties to agreement based on this 
standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility 
of applying the most recent editions of the standards 
indicated below: 

IS No. Title 

264 : 1976 Nitric acid (second revision) 

265 : 1993 Hydrochloric acid (fourih revision) 
1 070 : 1 992 Reagent grade water (third revision) 
2112: 2002 Silver jewellery/artefacts — Fineness 

and hallmarking 

3 TERMINOLOGY 

3.0 For the purpose of this standard, the following 
defmitions shall apply. 



3.1 Assay Unit 

Assay unit equivalent to 1.219 2 g is to be used. The 
weight of pure silver sample equivalent to this unit, 
also called "Assay Pound", will yield a cake of silver 
chloride weighing exactly 1.620 g. Silver chloride 
cakes of silver samples when weighed against 
Platinum-Iridium Assay- Weights specifically made for 
this purpose will facilitate direct determination of 
fineness of silver in part per thousand (96o). 

3.2 Silver Assay Weights 

Shall be of highest accuracy and of Platinum-Iridium 
alloy. The weight 1.620 g shall be stamped '*! 000" 
similarly all other standard weights shall be marked 
as 990, 980, 970 etc, which denotes the purity of silver 
samples directly in part per thousand (96o). 

3.3 Alternatively high precision top loading single pan 
balance capable of weighing to an accuracy of 
0.0 1 mg can be used. For calculation of silver in parts 
per thousand procedure given at 7.6 shall be used. 
While using such balances the weight of samples shall 
be I g for gravimetric methods (I and II) and 0.5 g for 
volumetric (potentiometric) method respectively. 

3.4 Check Silver 

Silver of known fineness but not less than 999 for 
jewellery articles or artefacts but for estimation of fine 
silver check silver shall be of 999.9 fineness. 

4 SAMPLING 

4.1 Dip Sampling 

A dip sample from the representative lot shall be taken 
with a sampler from the molten metal just before 
casting and granulated or cast into a button. This may 
be hammered, rolled, cleaned and cut into small pieces 
for assaying. 

4.2 Two samples shall be taken by cutting or drilling 
diagonally opposite comers from the upper and lower 
sides if the material is in the form of ingot, slab or 
bar. The samples shall then be cut into small pieces 
and thoroughly mixed together. 

NOTE — Iron particles, if any, may be separated with the help ot 
a magnate before wetghment of the sample. 



18 2113:2002 



4.3 When the material is in the form of sheets or wire, 
small pieces shall be cut preferably from opposite ends 
and thoroughly mixed together. 

4.4 In case of dispute with regard to sampling of ingots, 
slab, bar, sheet or wire, a dip sample shall be taken 
from the representative lot. 

4.5 Before taking samples by any of the above methods, 
all surface dirt from the article shall be removed and 
all instruments for cutting, scrapping, hammering, etc 
shall be cleaned thoroughly. No oil shall be used for 
drilling. 

4.6 The surface of the bar shall be well scrapped before 
sampling or the first portion of metal removed during 
the preparation of the sample shall be rejected if the 
bar has been pickled by dipping in acid after casting. 

4.7 For coated articles, appropriate precautions as 
agreed shall be taken to ensure exclusion of coating. 

5 QUALITY OF REAGENTS 

Unless specified otherwise, analytical grade chemical 
and reagent grade water shall be employed for the tests. 

6 GRAVIMETRIC METHOD (I) 

6.1 Apparatus 

6.1.1 Assay Balance 

It is a balance of highest precision, capable of 
weighing 2 g in each pan and sensitive to COS mg. 
The balance should be so adjusted that one division of 
the scale traversed by the pointer corresponds to 0. 1 
part per thousand (96o). 

6.1.2 Assay Bottle 

Assay bottles shall be made up of good, strong, clean 
glass capable of being heated on a hot plate without 
cracking. They shall be approximately 70 mm in 
diameter slightly tapered up to a height of 1 3 cm where 
they form a circular neck about 25 mm in height and 
20 mm outside diameter. Capacity shall be about 
350 ml and shall be fitted with a ground glass stopper 
which goes flush with the neck about 10 mm inside 
and has a spherical head outside. 

6.1.3 Drying Oven 

It must be capable of being regulated and maintained 
up to a temperature of 200 **C. 

6.1.4 Metallic Tray 

It should be of rectangular shape of two types, plain 
and the other with numbered regular depressions for 
carrying skiffs. 



6. 1.5 Potting Trough 

About 100 mm in depth and immune to dilute acids. 
They shall have collars of stainless steel or other 
suitable material fixed on the sides to hold the assay 
bottles in an inclined and inverted position. 

6.1.6 Shaking Machine 

Mechanically operated and consisting of a box which 
shall be capable of holding securely a number of assay 
bottles at a time and also capable of imparting vertical/ 
horizontal reciprocating movements to this box. 

6.1.7 Tongs and Forceps 

They should be of various forms for transferring the 
cups to and from the drying chamber, handling assay 
pieces, silver chloride cakes etc. 

6.1.8 Turn Table 

Heavy circular wooden table pivoted at the centre and 
capable of smooth rotation. 

6. 1 .9 Wedgwood Cups 

They shall be of conical shape of about 25 ml capacity 
and about 25 mm in height, standing on a base 25 mm 
in diameter widening into about 38 mm at the top. 

6. 1 . 1 Wedgwood Dishes 

Saucer-shaped, about 90 mm diameter at the top. 

6.1.11 Silver Assay Weights (see also 3.2) 

6.2 Reagents 

6.2.1 Dilute Nitric Acid 

Dilute 640 ml of concentrated nitric acid (p '■= 1 .42) 
with 1 520 ml of water. 

6.2.2 Dilute Hydrochloric Acid 

Dilute 320 ml concentrated hydrochloric acid 
(p= 1.16) with 1 840 ml of water. 

6.3 Procedure 

6.3.1 The assay shall be carried out by two assayers 
independently on duplicate samples. 

6.3.2 Weigh each silver sample against Assay Pound 
Weigh (that is, 1.219 2 g) in duplicate, accurately 
within division of the scale (note and allow for the 
correction in the final weighment of silver chloride) 
and transfer directly into clean assay bottle using a 
small metallic/plastic funnel for transfer. 

6.3.3 Dissolve in about 15 ml of nitric acid (6.2.1) 
and heat the bottle on a hot plate, until dissolution is 
complete. Expel nitrous fumes. If insoluble matter, 
for example, gold, tin, etc, are present, dilute the 



IS2113:2002 



solution with 10 ml of water and remove gold by 
filtration using Whattman filter paper No. 1 in case 
of gold is present. If tin is present, evaporate the 
contents on low heat to syrapy consistency to 
precipitate tin as metastannic acid precipitate to settle 
and then filter through a Whattman filter paper 
No. 42 with sufficient number of washings with 3 
percent nitric acid till the washing is free of silver. 
Dilute the solution with distilled water to about' ISO 
ml and add 10 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid (6.2.2) 
from a dropping pipette in one stroke. Stopper the 
bottle and shake vigorously for 2 min till the 
precipitated silver chloride coagulates and leaves a 
clear supernatant liquid. Remove the stopper carefully 
so as not to lose any chloride, test the solution in the 
bottle with a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid. 
When the precipitation is found to be complete, fill 
the bottle with distilled water up to the neck, stopper 
and give a gentle shake to distribute the silver chloride 
precipitate uniformly at the bottom. Allow it to stand 
for at least an hour. 

6.3.4 Siphon off the clear supernant solution 
containing the base metals to a height of 5 mm of 
solution with the help of a glass siphon, taking care 
not to loose any silver chloride precipitate. Add about 
2 ml of dilute nitric (6.2.1) and fill the bottle again 
with distilled water, stopper properly and stir with 
rotary motion and then give a gentle shake to distribute 
silver chloride uniformly at the bottom and allow to 
stand at least for 2 h or preferably over night in a dark 
place to settle down the precipitate. 

NoriiS 

1 In case, if lead is present, siphoning should be done hot. 

2 In case, if tin is present, it is preferable to take the sample in 
1 00 ml beaker for dissolution and follow as stated in 6.3 J. 

6.3.5 Transfer the precipitate into Wedgwood cup 
placed on Wedgwood dish and kept immersed in water 
on a glass plate in the tapping trough. Invert carefully 
the bottle containing the silver chloride precipitate over 
the cup so that the mouth of the bottle remains under 
the water while the precipitate is collected in the cup. 
Fix the bottle in an inclined position by the clip and 
rotate the bottle. Tap gently for 10 min to transfer the 
precipitate completely into the cup. Withdraw the 
bottle, and the cup with the saucer from the trough 
and transfer any particles of silver chloride precipitate 
found in the saucer into the cup. 

6.3.6 Decant ofTa little water from the cup, now full, 
taking care not to lose any chloride. Hold this gently 
between the thumb and tiie fore-finger of the left hand 
and tap the cup gently with the end of a thick glass 
rod covered with a rubber tube to spread out the 
chloride evenly. Allow it to settle for 5 min and drain 
off the water from the cup as completely as possible 
avoiding any loss of silver chloride from the cup while 



draining. Place the cup with the precipitate of silver 
chloride inside the oven and dry at 90°C for 1 h. Raise 
the temperature to 160X slowly within half an hour 
and held at the same temperature for 1 h. Lower the 
temperature to 120''C and take out the cups in 
convenient lots for weighment. 

6.3.7 While still warm, transfer the silver chloride 
cake directly from the cup with a Platinum tipped 
forceps to the removable pan of the balance, scrapping 
out gently any chloride particles sticking on the sides 
of the cup into the pan. Record the weights in part per 
thousand and reduce or increase the reading by the 
proportionate correction noted initially when the 
sample was weighed (6.3.2) depending upon the 
fineness of silver. 

6.3.8 Run simultaneously with the samples at least 
two assays with check silver (3.3) one at the beginning 
and the other at the end in order to serve as a guide to 
the proper working of the different stages of the 
procedure. 

6.4 Method of Reporting 

6.4.1 Weigh the silver chloride cake accurately in the 
assay balance using the corresponding standard silver 
weights and riders to get the accurate fineness of the 
sample and after applying necessary correction as 
given in 6.3.7. 

6.4.2 Record the mean value of the four test results 
[two results from each assayer (6.3.1)], provided the 
difTerence among them is not more than 0.8 part per 
thousand (PPT). 

6.4.3 In case one of the results is most divergent and 
other three are within 0.8 PPT, then the most divergent 
value is to be discarded and average of the other three 
values is to be reported. 

6.4.4 In case the difference between the average of 
close three values and the most divergent value is 
within 0.4 PPT, the average of all the four values shall 
be the fineness of the sample (parts per thousand). 

6.4.5 In all other cases all the four values should be 
individually reported. 

7 GRAVIMETRIC METHOD (II) 

7.1 Sampling 

As given in 4.1 to 4.7. 

7.2 Outline of the Method 

The sample is dissolved in nitric acid and silver is 
precipitated as silver chloride, filtered through 
previously weighed sintered glass crucible, wash, dried 
and weighed. 



IS 21 13: 2002 



7.3 Reagents 

7.3. 1 Dilute Nitric Acid [ 1 : 1 and 3:97 (v/v)] 

7.3.2 Dilute Hydrochloric Acid[\\9 (v/v)] 

lA Apparatus 

7.4.1 Balance of Accuracy, 0.01 mg. 

7.4.2 250 ml Glass Beakers 

7.4.3 75 mm Dia Watch Glasses 

7.4.4 Glass Rods Grounded at Both the End 

7.4.5 Sintered Glass Crucibles No, 3 (Medium Porosity) 
- 7.4.6 Wash Bottle with Fine Jet 

7.4.7 Filter Vacuum Pump 

7.4.8 Drying Oven (Electrical) up to 250°C 

7.4.9 Desiccator 

7.5 Procedure 

7.5.1 Weigh three Nos. of 1.00 g of each sample 
accurately up to 0.01 mg. Transfer into three Nos. of 
250 ml beakers. Add 1 5 ml of dilute nitric acid (1 : 1), 
cover the beakers with watch glass and heat gently on 
the hot plate till the samples are completely dissolved. 
Expel all the nitrous fumes. 

7.5.2 Remove the beakers from the hot plate and 
remove the watch glass by washing with a fine jet 
avoiding spurting. Dilute the content to about 100 ml 
with distilled water. Add 20 ml of hydrochloric acid 
to it slowly with continuous stirring avoiding any loss 
of silver chloride while stirring. Cover the beakers 
with watch glass and keep the beakers on hot plate, 
avoiding boiling. After 1 h check with few drops of 
dilute hydrochloric for the complete precipitation of 
silver. Keep on the hot plate at least for 2 h (preferably 
over night in a dark place). 

7.5.3 Remove the watch glass from the beakers while 
washing very gently with a fine jet of reagent grade 
water, wash down the walls of the beaker with fine 
jet, and filter through previously cleaned, dried and 
weighed sintered glass crucible using vacuum 
pump (7.4.7). Adjust the rate of filtration, by adjusting 
the pressure of the pump so that it is neither too fast 
nor too slow. Wash the precipitate 2-3 times with dilute 
nitric acid (3 percent) and then S to 6 times with 
distilled water. 

7.5.4 Dry the sintered glass crucibles with silver 
chloride precipitate in electric oven (7.4.8) at 140^C 
for at least 1 h. Cool the crucibles in desiccator (7.4.8) 
to room temperature and weight after 1 h. Repeat 
the procedure till constant weight is obtained. 



7.6 Calculations 



Silver, part per thousand = —x 0.752 6x10' 



where 

A ~ Mass in g of silver chloride, and 
B = Mass in g of the sample. 

NOTES 

1 After dissolutton of the samples (7.5.2) in nitric acid if gold is 
present, filter through a Whattman filter paper No. I and wash the 
filter paper containing gold several times with water till washing 
is free from silver. 

2 In case tin is present, evaporate the contents on low heat to syrupy 
consistency to precipitate tin as meta stannic acid. Add S ml of nitric 
acid and 20 ml water and allow the beaker to stand on hot plate to 
settle down the precipitate. Filter the precipitate through Whattman 
filter paper No. 42, wash the precipitate at least five-six times with 
nitric acid till the washing is free from silver. Continue the 
precipitation of silver with hydrochloric acid as in 7.5.2. 

7.7 Repeatability 

Duplicate and quadruplicate determinations shall give 
results differing by not more than O.S and 1 .0 parts 
per thousand (%o) respectively by mass for silver alloys 
and not more than 0.2 and 0.4 parts per thousand (%o) 
respectively for fine silver. When the difference is 
greater than this assay shall be repeated. 

8 DETERMINATION OF SILVER IN SILVER 
ALLOYS BY VOLULMETRIC(POTENTIOMETRIQ 
METHOD USING SODIUM CHLORIDE OR 
POTASSIUM CHLORIDE 

8.1 Principle 

The sample is dissolved in dilute nitric acid. The silver 
content of the resulting solution is determined by 
titration with standard sodium chloride or potassium 
chloride solution using potentiometric indication of 
the equivalence point. 

8.2 REAGENTS 

8.2.1 Nitric Acid, 33 percent (v/v) (sp. gr; 1 .200) Free 
of halide. 

8.2.2 Sodium Chloride Solution (0.25 mol/litre) 

Dissolve 14.6 g of Sodium chloride (dried at 105°C) 
in water and dilute to I 000 ml. 

8.2.3 Potassium Chloride Solution (0.25 mol/litre) 

Dissolve 1 8.6 gofpotassium chloride (dried at I05''C) 
in water and dilute to 1 000 ml. 

8.2.4 Check Disodium Dimethylglyoxime Octahydrate 
Solution 

Dissolve 10 g of disodium dimethylglyoxime 
octahydrate in 1 000 ml of water. 



IS2113:2002 



8.2.5 Silver, Minimum Purity 999.9 parts per 
thousand (%o) by mass. 

8.3 Apparatus 

8.3.1 Ordinary Laboratory Glassware and Apparatus 

8.3.2 Motor driven plunger or piston-type burette 
linked to potentiometer, preferably an automatic 
titrator capable of delivering increment of 0.05 ml at 
the equivalence point. 

8.3.3 Titration apparatus with combination silver 
electrode or silver chloride coated silver electrode and 
Hg/Hgj SO^ electrode or other suitable reference 
electrode. 

8.3.4 Titration beaker with automatic titrator. 

NOTB — It is preferable to use automatic titrator to get accurate 
and reproducible result within limit of tolerance. 

9 PROCEDURE 

9.1 Test Portion 

The mass of sample used for the titration shall contain 
between 300 mg and 500 mg of silver and shall be 
weighed to an accuracy of 0.01 mg. 

9.2 Determination of Sodium Chloride or Potassium 
Chloride Standard Solution Factor 

9.2.1 Preparation of Silver Standards 

Weigh to the nearest 0.01 mg, three samples, each of 
300 mg to 500 mg of silver and transfer them to glass 
beakers. Add 5 ml of nitric acid (8.2.1) to each, and 
warm gently (preferably in water bath) to dissolve the 
silver. Keep the tops of the beakers covered with watch 
glasses. Heat until evolution of nitrogen oxides ceases. 
Allow it to cool. Rinse the watch glasses into beakers. 
Transfer to the titration beaker (8.3.4). Add the 
minimum volume of water, within the range of about 
20 ml to 60 ml to satisfy the requirements of the 
titration apparatus (8.3.3) with respect to measurement 
and stirring. 

N01 H — The mass of the standard silver samples should lie within 
20 mg of the mass of silver in the test samples. 

9.2.2 Titration of Standard Silver Solution 

Add via the plunger-burette and with continuous 
stirring, sufficient sodium chloride (8.2.2) or 
potassium chloride (8.2.3) to precipitate about 
90 percent of silver in silver solution. Titrate the 
remaining silver in such a manner that the equivalence 
point can be interpolated from 0.050 ml additions of 
sodium chloride solution. 

NOTLi — This split titration approach may be effected 
automatically using an automatic titrator with so called dynamic 
volume dosing based on the measured potential difference across 
the electrodes in the titration apparatus (8 J J). 



9.2.3 Calculation of Sodium Chloride or Potassium 
Chloride Factor 

The sodium chloride or potassium chloride factor F, is 
calculated using the formula: 

K 
where 

m^ = mass of silver in milligrams, and 
K = volume in millilitres of sodium chloride 
or potassium chloride solution at the 
equivalence point. 
The factor determinations should not differ from each 
other by more than 0.05 parts per hundred (percent) 
relative value. 

The mean value F, shall be used in subsequent 
calculations for maximum accuracy. The sodium 
chloride or potassium chloride factor shall be 
determined immediately before analysis of the test 
samples. 

9.3 Determination 

9.3.1 Preparation of Test Solutions 

Weigh two test samples each containing between 
300 mg to 500 mg silver to an accuracy of 0.01 mg 
and transfer into glass beaker or titration beaker with 
automatic titrator. Add 5 ml of nitric acid (8.2.1). Keep 
the beakers covered with watch glasses, fleat until 
evolution of nitrogen oxides ceases. Allow to cool. 
Rinse the water glasses into the respective beakers. 
Transfer the solution to titration apparatus (8.3.3). Add 
water as per 9.2.1. 

NOTE — When Teflon beaker, supplied with automatic titrator 
is used along with hot water bath for dissolution of samples it can 
be directly fixed in the titration apparatus. 

9.3.2 Elimination of Palladium 

Palladium shall be eliminated by addition of an 
aqueous solution of disodium dimethylglyoxime 
octahydrate (8.2.4). For each 100 mg Palladium add 
20 ml of this solution and stir before commencing 
titration. 

9.3.3 Titration of Test Solution 

Proceed exactly as per the standard solution. It may 
be necessary to carryout a pilot determination to obtain 
an approximate value of the silver content.

Since the sodium chloride or potassium chloride factor 
F(9.2) is expressed in milligrams of silver for each 
milliliter of solution, the mass /w^^, in milligrams, of

silver in the test portion is caltulated using the where 
formula:

Bureau of Indian Standards 

BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote 
harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods 
and attending to connected matters in the country. 

Copyright 

BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any form 
without the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of 
implementing the standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. 
Enquiries relating to copyright be addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. 

Review of Indian Standards 

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 
'BIS Catalogue' and 'Standards: Monthly Additions'. 

This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc : No. MTD 10 (4378).
